why: The three worked tests are the evidence that produces the closing recommendation.
The computational half of "mutual validation" is the simulated null hypothesis built in Chapter 9: a test statistic, a null hypothesis model, and a p-value counted from simulated results.
The quantity both methods estimate is the sampling distribution, constructed by resampling before any formula appears; standard error is defined as its standard deviation.
Recognising a heavy-tailed column requires the theoretical distributions of Chapter 5; the lognormal and Pareto counterexamples are meaningless without them.
The failures of the CLT are demonstrated with normal probability plots, not with test statistics.

Chapter 14's t test recomputes exactly the pregnancy-length comparison Chapter 9 solved by pooling and shuffling; the resampled and analytic p-values are compared (0.170 analytic vs ttest_ind 0.1676).

The correlation test replaces the Chapter 9 permutation test for correlation between birth weight and mother's age; the analytic method buys a precise small p-value (5.72e-11) that resampling could only bound below 0.001.
The chi-squared test replaces the Chapter 9 crooked-die proportion test; the analytic and SciPy p-values agree at 0.0407.
Pearson correlation, standard scores, and rank correlation are defined in Chapter 7; the correlation test tests the statistic defined there.
Chapter 8 obtains sd/sqrt(n) empirically by resampling penguin weights; Chapter 14 derives the same expression from the algebra of normal distributions.
Comparing an empirical CDF with a model CDF is the book's standard fit check; the CDF is defined and used for comparison in Chapter 4.
Pmf and Cdf are shown to be interconvertible, which is what makes CDF-against-model comparison a valid test rather than a shape coincidence.
Chapter 5 explicitly names Chapter 14 as the destination: theoretical distributions "lend themselves to mathematical analysis, as we'll see in Chapter 14."
Neither method rescues a biased sample; Chapter 8 states that sampling variability is only one source of error and often not the biggest.
Cheap analytic p-values are not the goal: Chapter 11 shows a statistically significant relationship that barely improves prediction.
Before any test, Chapter 1 validates NSFG variables against published tables and transforms raw codes; an unvalidated column makes every downstream p-value meaningless.
